title: Repair or Replace: The Factors That Actually Decide
description: A framework for deciding whether to repair or replace a phone or appliance - repair cost ratios, remaining lifespan and reliability risk.
content:
The "50% rule" (repair above half the replacement price is not worth it) is repeated everywhere and is both too simple and backwards: the right comparison is not repair cost versus sticker price, but cost per remaining month of service on each side of the decision.

## The comparison that matters

Two options, each with a cost and an expected service duration:

- **Repair**: price of the fix, expected additional months of life after the fix.
- **Replace**: price of the new device (minus resale of the old one if any), expected months of life of the new device.

Cost per month = cost ÷ expected months. The lower number wins on economics alone. A $180 battery-and-screen repair buying two more years (24 months) is $7.50/month. A $700 replacement lasting four years (48 months) is $14.58/month — the repair wins despite costing a third of the replacement's sticker.

The 50% rule fails because it ignores remaining lifespan on both sides: repair can be the bargain even at 70% of replacement price if it extends life close to a replacement's, and replacement can be right even at 30% if the repaired device will fail again next month.

## Estimating the durations honestly

- **After repair**: what failed? Batteries and screens are wear items with predictable outcomes — a replaced battery behaves like new. A repair of a systemic issue (recurring board faults) buys less certainty. Check whether the repair carries its own warranty; a 12-month warranty sets a floor on your expected months.
- **After replacement**: honest use-life for your pattern — flagship phones often serve 4–5 years, laptops 5–7 with a battery swap inside. Discount the estimate if your workload grows faster than hardware does.
- **Risk adjustment**: the older device carries unknown failure probability. If a second failure would be catastrophic (no backup device, critical work), weight reliability above the pure arithmetic.

## Factors the arithmetic does not capture

**Data and setup friction.** Migrating a phone or rebuilding a laptop environment has real time cost and risk. It is usually small for phones (cloud restore) and large for specialized workstations.

**Feature drift.** A repaired three-year-old device keeps three-year-old capabilities: slower chip, older camera, fewer network bands. Sometimes acceptable, sometimes the actual reason you are dissatisfied.

**Software support.** If the device is near the end of its update window, a repair extends hardware life into software insecurity. Check the update policy before repairing a device in its final year.

**Environmental weight.** Extending a device's life defers manufacturing emissions and e-waste; replacement demand also drives availability of parts and better trade-in programs, so this factor is genuinely two-sided. As a tie-breaker rather than a decider, keeping a working device longer usually has the lighter footprint.

**Resale and warranty.** A device with remaining resale value makes replacement less costly; a device under warranty makes repair nearly free. Subtract both from their respective sides.

## The decision sequence

1. Get the actual repair quote — not a forum estimate.
2. Estimate months gained after repair (warranty as floor; component type as context).
3. Price replacement net of resale; estimate its months.
4. Compute cost per month on both sides; apply risk and software-support adjustments.
5. Check the non-financial list: setup friction, feature drift, backup availability.

## When to ignore all of it

If the device frustrates you for reasons a repair will not address (too big, wrong camera, unsupported app), you are not solving a failure — you are changing products. That is a purchasing decision: run it through your normal criteria instead. Conversely, when economics are close, repair usually wins on hassle alone: no migration, no learning curve, no unbundled accessories to repurchase.

## Worked examples

**Phone with a dead battery.** Repair quote $120, expected two more years of use after the fix (24 months): $5.00/month. Replacement $699, expected four years (48 months): $14.56/month. Repair wins on economics. If the same phone also has a cracked screen that affects resale, add the screen cost to the repair side and re-run the division.

**Laptop with a failed hinge.** Repair $250, but the machine is already four years old and the battery will likely need replacing within a year — expected remaining life after repair maybe 18 months: $13.89/month. Replacement $1,100 with a five-year horizon (60 months): $18.33/month. Repair still wins on the pure arithmetic, but if the hinge failure signals broader chassis wear, risk-adjust the 18-month estimate downward before deciding.

**Appliance with an intermittent fault.** A $90 call-out that may or may not fix the problem has an expected months figure that includes the probability of failure returning. If the technician gives a 50% chance of a lasting fix and the post-fix life is 36 months, expected months = 0.5 × 36 = 18, so effective cost per month doubles. Compare that against replacement before agreeing to the repair.

## What to collect before you call anyone

- The exact model number — repair quotes vary widely for near-identical models.
- A written quote that separates parts from labour, and states whether the fix carries a warranty.
- The price of a comparable replacement including any accessories you would need to re-buy (charger, case, docks).
- Your honest remaining-use estimate: would you keep the device for the full expected life, or upgrade sooner for other reasons?
